MemoryAutonomyKnowledge

Memory needs boundaries.

Separate task state from long-term preferences; define ownership, correction, and permission to reuse information.

INDUSTRY PERSPECTIVE & CAREER DIRECTION

Autonomy needs
a stopping point.

Support integration and trip planning raise the same product question: which decisions can the system make, and which still belong to a person?

01 / AUTONOMY

Expand scope by risk.

Document retrieval can run within approved access. A refund changes business state: action gates must check authority, conditions, and execution status. Model confidence cannot authorize it. Irreversible actions need a named approver.

Support architecture
02 / EVALS & COORDINATION

Make collaboration earn its cost.

Parallel travel research helps only when the final itinerary stays consistent. Start with a single planner; add specialists for independent research. Task-level evals compare constraints, recovery, cost, and latency. Permission violations remain a separate release blocker.

Trip planning architecture
03 / MEMORY

Remember less. Keep it current.

Trip state, personal preferences, and company policy have different lifetimes. Retain preferences with permission; keep sources and versions with evidence. Corrections, deletions, and access changes must invalidate old context. Evals should replay these changes across sessions.

Document Q&A architecture

Customer support agent integration
INTEGRATED AT GTSP

AI support, connected to the business

Integrated a customer support agent for company-document Q&A, refunds, and order changes, from request classification to tool integration and acceptance checks.

Responsibilities and key decisions
Scope
Separated document questions, order lookups, business changes, and human handling; defined the automation boundary and handoff points.
Integration and state
Wrapped existing business APIs as agent tools with explicit inputs, permission checks, and error responses. Separated requested, awaiting confirmation, completed, and exceptional states, preserving context for human handoff.
Key decision
Separated model proposals from authorized execution. Checked execution status after timeouts before retrying, and attributed failures to retrieval, policy interpretation, or tool execution before selecting improvements.
Acceptance: answers, permissions, and failures
  • Answers and evidenceChecked agreement with source documents, citation support, and limitation disclosure or handoff for missing, conflicting, or outdated information.
  • Permissions and approvalChecked rejection of changes to another user’s order, protection of order information, and named approval before irreversible execution.
  • Retries and handoffChecked execution state and duplicate side effects under timeouts and repeated submissions; checked handoff context for the request, evidence, attempted actions, and unresolved issue.

Architecture notes: Retrieval, permissions, and evaluation proposals extend the delivered integration.

Approval boundaries across four workflows

Workflow design examples.

Demand desk

Recommend a product for the customer’s occasion, generate a try-on image, and prepare a shopping list.

Human approval before payment.
Knowledge desk

Answer from an approved document collection, cite sources, and propose knowledge-base updates.

Human approval before document updates.
Attention desk

Prioritize incoming messages, draft replies in two tones, and escalate requests beyond the agent’s authority.

Human approval before sending.
Exception desk

Prioritize exceptions, recommend a response under business rules, and draft a case record.

Human approval before financial actions.

Answers with visible data freshness.

Source updateETL → storageVersion-aware cacheCited answer

HOW I THINKA REUSABLE FRAMEWORK

A practical design framework.

A good architecture connects a product objective to decisions that can be inspected and tested.

  1. Clarify requirements
  2. Define LLM objectives
  3. Draw system boundaries
  4. Design the architecture
  5. Evaluate
  6. Validate release readiness

Architecture follows the problem: RAG, agents, multimodal systems, reasoning — or a combination.

01

Autonomy is a design choice.

Workflow vs. agent: choose the right level of autonomy. Design tool use, state, human review, fallback, and escalation together.

02

Evals come first.

Define what “good” looks like, build an eval dataset, find which stage fails, and test whether a change actually improves the product.

03

Decisions need evidence.

Every architecture choice names the alternatives considered and why each was or was not chosen. Make the trade-offs reviewable.

A SHARED DECISION PROCESS

Product and engineering collaboration.

Turn ambiguous requirements into architecture decisions that a team can evaluate, discuss, and revise.

  1. Frame the product question.Clarify user needs, constraints, success criteria, and the cost of getting it wrong.
  2. Make alternatives reviewable.Map system boundaries and compare options with explicit assumptions and trade-offs.
  3. Agree on evidence.Define evaluation cases, ownership, release gates, and escalation before increasing autonomy.
